{{Short description|Part of the theory of modular forms}}
In mathematics,  '''Atkin–Lehner theory''' is part of the theory of [[modular form]]s describing when they arise at a given integer ''level'' ''N'' in such a way that the theory of [[Hecke operator]]s can be extended to higher levels.

Atkin–Lehner theory is based on the concept of a '''newform''', which is a [[cusp form]] 'new' at a given ''level'' ''N'', where the levels are the nested [[congruence subgroup]]s:
:<math>\Gamma_0(N) = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} \in \text{SL}(2, \mathbf{Z}): c \equiv 0 \pmod{N} \right\}</math>
of the [[modular group]], with ''N'' ordered by [[divisibility]]. That is, if ''M'' divides ''N'',  Γ<sub>0</sub>(''N'') is a [[subgroup]] of Γ<sub>0</sub>(''M''). The '''oldforms''' for Γ<sub>0</sub>(''N'') are those modular forms ''f''(''&tau;'') of level ''N'' of the form ''g''(''d &tau;'') for modular forms ''g'' of level ''M'' with ''M'' a proper divisor of ''N'', where ''d'' divides ''N/M''. The newforms are defined as a vector subspace of the modular forms of level ''N'', complementary to the space spanned by the oldforms, i.e. the orthogonal space with respect to the [[Petersson inner product]].

The [[Hecke operator]]s, which act on the space of all cusp forms, preserve the subspace of newforms and are [[self-adjoint operator|self-adjoint]] and commuting operators (with respect to the Petersson inner product) when restricted to this subspace. Therefore, the algebra of operators on newforms they generate is a finite-dimensional [[C*-algebra]] that is commutative; and by the [[spectral theorem|spectral theory]] of such operators, there exists a basis for the space of newforms consisting of eigenforms for the full [[Hecke algebra]].

==Atkin–Lehner involutions==
Consider a [[Hall divisor]] ''e'' of ''N'', which means that not only does ''e'' divide ''N'', but also ''e'' and ''N''/''e'' are relatively prime (often denoted ''e''||''N''). If ''N'' has ''s'' distinct prime divisors, there are 2<sup>''s''</sup> Hall divisors of ''N''; for example, if ''N'' = 360 = 2<sup>3</sup>⋅3<sup>2</sup>⋅5<sup>1</sup>, the 8 Hall divisors of ''N'' are 1, 2<sup>3</sup>, 3<sup>2</sup>, 5<sup>1</sup>, 2<sup>3</sup>⋅3<sup>2</sup>, 2<sup>3</sup>⋅5<sup>1</sup>, 3<sup>2</sup>⋅5<sup>1</sup>, and 2<sup>3</sup>⋅3<sup>2</sup>⋅5<sup>1</sup>.

For each Hall divisor ''e'' of ''N'', choose an integral matrix ''W''<sub>''e''</sub> of the form 
:<math>W_e = \begin{pmatrix}ae & b \\ cN & de \end{pmatrix}</math>
with det ''W''<sub>''e''</sub> = ''e''. These matrices have the following properties:
* The elements ''W''<sub>''e''</sub> ''normalize'' Γ<sub>0</sub>(''N''): that is, if ''A'' is in Γ<sub>0</sub>(''N''), then ''W''<sub>''e''</sub>''AW''{{su|b=''e''|p=−1}} is in Γ<sub>0</sub>(''N'').
* The matrix ''W''{{su|b=''e''|p=2}}, which has determinant ''e''<sup>2</sup>, can be written as ''eA'' where ''A'' is in Γ<sub>0</sub>(''N''). We will be interested in operators on [[cusp form]]s coming from the action of ''W''<sub>''e''</sub> on Γ<sub>0</sub>(''N'') by conjugation, under which both the scalar ''e'' and the matrix ''A'' act trivially. Therefore, the equality ''W''{{su|b=''e''|p=2}} = ''eA'' implies that the action of ''W''<sub>''e''</sub> squares to the identity; for this reason, the resulting operator is called an '''Atkin–Lehner involution'''.
* If ''e'' and ''f'' are both Hall divisors of ''N'', then W<sub>''e''</sub> and W<sub>''f''</sub> commute modulo Γ<sub>0</sub>(''N''). Moreover, if we define ''g'' to be the Hall divisor ''g'' = ''ef''/(''e'',''f'')<sup>2</sup>, their product is equal to W<sub>''g''</sub> modulo Γ<sub>0</sub>(''N'').
* If we had chosen a different matrix ''W'' ′<sub>''e''</sub> instead of ''W''<sub>''e''</sub>, it turns out that ''W''<sub>''e''</sub> ≡ ''W'' ′<sub>''e''</sub> modulo Γ<sub>0</sub>(''N''), so ''W''<sub>''e''</sub> and ''W'' ′<sub>''e''</sub> would determine the same Atkin–Lehner involution.
We can summarize these properties as follows. Consider the subgroup of GL(2,'''Q''') generated by Γ<sub>0</sub>(''N'') together with the matrices ''W''<sub>''e''</sub>; let Γ<sub>0</sub>(''N'')<sup>+</sup> denote its quotient by positive scalar matrices. Then Γ<sub>0</sub>(''N'') is a [[normal subgroup]] of Γ<sub>0</sub>(''N'')<sup>+</sup> of index 2<sup>''s''</sup> (where ''s'' is the number of distinct prime factors of ''N''); the [[quotient group]] is isomorphic to ('''Z'''/2'''Z''')<sup>s</sup> and acts on the cusp forms via the Atkin–Lehner involutions.
